problem: Embodied visual tracking (EVT) methods are mostly single-agent imitation learners that depend on costly expert data and static training environments, so they generalize poorly and are brittle under active interference. RL for language-conditioned EVT with VLA models is barely studied, and existing benchmarks only test idealized or passively disturbed settings.
motivation: Competition drives capability evolution in humans and animals, because opponents' changing strategies keep raising task difficulty. A competing agent in the scene can act as an adaptive environment that supplies an automatic, escalating curriculum. Existing EVT benchmarks lack active adversaries, so robustness to intentional interference cannot be measured.
key_idea: Train a VLA tracker with GRPO in a competitive two-agent game in which an opponent robot, with an asymmetric reward, contends for the same target, and evaluate it on a new competitive-tracking benchmark.
insight: Multi-agent RL beats single-agent RL and SFT-only on EVT-Bench STT (SR 92.1 vs 89.5 vs 88.2, CR 0.9 vs 2.2 vs 3.1), so adaptive opponents provide a more informative training signal than a static environment. The opponent-strength study shows a static obstacle gives marginal gains and random interference even degrades performance, while a competitive tracking opponent gives the best gains. So the benefit comes from a strategic, adaptive adversary, not from mere disturbance. The result also suggests that the training paradigm, more than model scale, explains the gain of a 3B model over 7B baselines.
method: Backbone VLA: Qwen2.5VL-3B with a flow-matching action head that regresses 5 waypoints (x,y,θ). Text is decoded autoregressively and navigation tasks are triggered by a <Nav> token.

SFT stage: inputs are 4-view current frames plus a sliding-window history of front views, compressed by multi-scale grid pooling (fine tokens for recent frames, coarse for older). Loss is MSE on waypoints plus α·cross-entropy on text, trained on tracking, navigation and VQA data.

Single-agent GRPO: reward is a Gaussian distance term (optimum 2.25 m, σ=0.75), plus facing and persistence bonuses and sparse terminal success/failure/collision rewards. It uses group advantage over T_group=10, a clipped ratio, an entropy bonus and a KL penalty to the SFT policy. Only LoRA adapters on the LLM are trained.

Competitive multi-agent RL: a tracker and an opponent quadruped, both initialized from the SFT checkpoint, are rolled out simultaneously. The opponent competes for the same target and interferes via occlusion, path crossing and blocking. Each agent is optimized with GRPO on its own returns.
Asymmetric rewards: the opponent's Gaussian distance optimum is shifted closer (1.25 m) to force contention. The tracker keeps the standard reward plus an opponent-aware safety/collision term.

CoMaTrack-Bench: STT episodes from EVT-Bench (HM3D/MP3D) with a second robot dog placed 0.5 m ahead of the tracker. Three opponent types are defined: static obstacle, random interference, and competitive tracking (the SFT policy as the opponent).

Data recipe: tracking data (6913 STT, 6685 DT, 6524 AT episodes), ScanQA, LLaVA-Pretrain, SYNTH-PEDES, RefCOCO, Flickr30k, and navigation data (R2R-CE, RxR-CE, YouTube-style data, HM3D ObjectNav, OVON).

setting.backbone: Qwen2.5VL-3B with flow-matching action head (SFT then GRPO with LoRA)
setting.training_data: SFT for 1 epoch on 48 H20 GPUs with EVT-Bench tracking episodes (6913 STT, 6685 DT, 6524 AT), navigation data (R2R-CE, RxR-CE, YouTube-style, HM3D ObjectNav, OVON), and VQA data (ScanQA, LLaVA-Pretrain, SYNTH-PEDES, RefCOCO, Flickr30k). Then 1 epoch of multi-agent GRPO on tracking data only, on 4 L20 GPUs.
setting.observation: 4-view egocentric monocular RGB (front, rear, left, right) plus history of front frames and a language instruction
setting.action_space: predicted relative waypoints (x, y, θ), 5 per step, from a flow-matching head
setting.privileged: none at test time (the opponent and reward signals are used only in training)

numbers.extra: SFT then competitive multi-agent GRPO; baselines are 7B
Zero-shot on the paper's own new benchmark; only Uni-NaVid (SR 42.4) was compared

numbers_note: The ablation table does not name the benchmark. Its Multi-Agent RL row (92.1/90.3/0.9) matches the EVT-Bench STT result, so it was assumed to be STT. The opponent-strength study is only in a figure (no numbers). EVT-Bench split labeled 'test' by assumption, since the paper does not name it.
results: A 3B CoMaTrack model reaches SR 92.1/74.2/57.5 on EVT-Bench STT/DT/AT. It slightly beats the strongest 7B baseline TrackVLA++ (90.9/74.0/55.9) and has clearly higher TR and lower CR. On CoMaTrack-Bench it gets SR 85.0 vs 42.4 for Uni-NaVid.
limitations: Validated only on EVT; there is no large-scale evaluation on broader VLN tasks such as instruction following or object navigation.
Opponent strategies are bounded by simulated priors and may not reflect real-world dynamics, and multi-agent training is costly and unstable due to non-stationarity.
Only Uni-NaVid is compared on CoMaTrack-Bench, and the EVT-Bench gains over TrackVLA++ are small (e.g. DT 74.2 vs 74.0). Real-world results are qualitative only.
